name: Hyperledger
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Hyperledger: Enterprise Blockchain's Open Source Toolbox
lesson.summary: Hyperledger is an open source umbrella project hosting a family of frameworks for building permissioned, enterprise blockchain networks, rather than a single blockchain itself.
lesson.body:
Hyperledger is not a blockchain in the way Bitcoin or Ethereum are. It is an umbrella open source project, hosted by the Linux Foundation since it was founded in December 2015, that develops a family of frameworks and tools organizations use to build their own permissioned, enterprise oriented blockchain networks. Where the previous chapters described private and consortium blockchains as governance models, Hyperledger is one of the main places those models actually get implemented in working software.

The most prominent project under the Hyperledger umbrella is Hyperledger Fabric, a modular permissioned blockchain framework in which every participating organization runs known, identified nodes rather than anonymous ones. Fabric supports pluggable consensus mechanisms, letting an implementer choose the agreement protocol that fits their needs instead of being locked into one, and it introduces channels, which let a defined subset of participants transact privately within a larger network without exposing those transactions to every other member. That last feature maps directly onto the consortium pattern from the previous chapter: a group of banks on a shared Fabric network could use channels so that two of them settle a bilateral trade without broadcasting the details to every other bank on the network.

Hyperledger is not just Fabric, though. Hyperledger Besu is an Ethereum compatible client, meaning it speaks the same protocol as Ethereum and can run smart contracts written for it, but it can be configured to run as either a public network participant or, notably, as the validator set for a private, permissioned network, blending the programmability of Ethereum style smart contracts with permissioned governance. Hyperledger Sawtooth is another modular permissioned framework with its own consensus options, and Hyperledger Indy focuses specifically on decentralized digital identity rather than general transactions. The pattern across all of them is the same: Hyperledger is a toolbox of building blocks that different industries, supply chain tracking, trade finance, healthcare records, adapt to their own permissioned or private network needs, rather than a single chain everyone joins.

Because Hyperledger frameworks are almost always deployed as private or consortium networks with a known, limited set of validators, they typically skip the expensive proof of work mining that permissionless networks rely on. Instead they use faster crash fault tolerant or byzantine fault tolerant consensus protocols, which are well suited to a small group of identified participants and do not need to defend against anonymous Sybil attackers the way a public network does, since every validator's identity and reputation is already known and accountable.

Worth noting for anyone researching this further: in 2024 the Linux Foundation reorganized the effort under a broader name, LF Decentralized Trust, reflecting a wider scope beyond the original Hyperledger branding, though the individual project names such as Fabric and Besu have continued under that umbrella.
